extracted.intended_audience: Florida administrative-law practitioners, agency counsel, and parties considering or litigating challenges to proposed Florida administrative rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the statutory 'points of entry' and related procedural/standing limitations for filing challenges to proposed Florida administrative rules under Fla. Stat. ch. 120, in light of Fla. Pulp & Paper. Explains triggers (notice, public hearing, SERC, notice of change/correction) and practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: First point of entry — 21 days after publication of notice of intended action
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition alleging invalidity of a proposed rule shall be filed within 21 days after the date of publication of the notice required by s. 120.54(3)(a). Publication of the notice of intended action initiates the adoption process and triggers the first point of entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the earliest and uniform trigger; a prudent challenger should consider filing at this first available opportunity. The statutory text ties this window directly to the notice of intended action published in the Florida Administrative Register (FAR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second point of entry — 10 days after the final public hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition may be filed within 10 days after the final public hearing is held on the proposed rule as provided by s. 120.54(3)(e)2. The term 'public hearing' is broadly defined to include 'any public meeting held by any agency at which the rule is considered.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because an agency is only required to schedule a hearing if an affected party requests one within 21 days of notice, adoption may occur without any public hearing (leaving this window unopened). Unlike the other windows, neither the APA nor the uniform rules contain an explicit notice requirement for the occurrence of the 'final' public hearing; requiring such notice could improve clarity but may be impractical when agencies cannot know a hearing is 'final' until it concludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third point of entry — 20 days after preparation/making available of SERC or revised SERC
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition may be filed within 20 days after the statement of estimated regulatory costs (SERC) or a revised SERC has been prepared and made available as provided in s. 120.541(1)(d). Agencies must prepare a SERC in certain circumstances (e.g., adverse impact on small business or costs likely to exceed $200,000 in a year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'revised SERC' that is prepared and made available triggers this window even if the revision is a change in narrative or reasons for rejecting alternatives (the court rejected a narrow reading that only cost-quantity changes count). However, challenges grounded in SERC procedure are subject to a one-year limitation from the effective date of the rule (120.541(1)(f)) and generally require the challenger to be 'substantially affected' by the rule's regulatory costs. Failure to respond to a LCRA or to prepare required SERCs can constitute a material procedural failure and an invalid exercise of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on SERC-based challenges and use of LCRA/120.52(8)(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: 120.541(1)(g) restricts a challenger's ability to invalidate a rule based on 120.52(8)(f) (that a rule imposes costs reducible by less costly alternatives) unless the challenger: (1) raises the issue in an administrative proceeding within one year of the effective date of the rule; (2) contests the agency's rejection of a lower cost regulatory alternative (LCRA); and (3) has substantial interests materially affected by that rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve a 120.52(8)(f)-type challenge, a substantially affected person should timely present the LCRA and prosecute any contest of the agency's rejection within the one-year window; otherwise remedial options to invalidate on cost-alternative grounds are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth point of entry — 20 days after publication of notice of change
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition may be filed within 20 days after the date of publication of the notice required by s. 120.54(3)(d). Section 120.54(3)(d) gives agencies three post-hearing options: (1) notify JAPC if no change; (2) notify JAPC if only technical/nonsubstantive change; or (3) file and publish a notice of change in the FAR if there was a nontechnical/substantive change. The fourth point is tied to publication of a notice of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person was not substantially affected by the proposed rule as initially noticed but becomes substantially affected as a result of a change, that person may challenge any provision of the resulting proposed rule. Conversely, a person who was substantially affected by the initially proposed rule but waits to challenge after a notice of change is generally limited to challenging only the changed provisions — requiring comparison of strike-through/underline versions to identify changes. This creates practical difficulty in parsing what actually changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing vs. timeliness — do not conflate 'substantially affected' with timeliness requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The court rejected importing an additional 'premature burden of standing' into the timeliness requirements of 120.56(2)(a). The issues of standing (whether a challenger is substantially affected) and timeliness (which point of entry is invoked) are distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challengers should analyze standing and timeliness separately. The First DCA held that failing to use an earlier point of entry does not necessarily preclude using a later one; statutory points of entry are 'mutually exclusive alternatives' separated by 'or.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a 'revised SERC' — narrative revisions may suffice to trigger third window
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'revised SERC' as contemplated by 120.541(1)(a) may include revision to the 'statement of the reasons for rejecting the alternative in favor of the proposed rule' and is not limited to revisions that change the numeric estimated costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies that prepare and make available a SERC revision (even a narrative change) will likely trigger the third point of entry; challengers and agencies should treat SERC 'revisions' broadly unless and until statute or controlling precedent narrows the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency failure to prepare/respond to SERC/LCRA is a material procedural defect
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's failure to respond to a submitted LCRA or failure to prepare a required SERC constitutes a material failure to follow required procedures and can amount to an invalid exercise of delegated legislative authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such procedural failures can be the substantive basis for a validity challenge, but statutory limits (e.g., one-year limitation, requirement of being substantially affected) and procedural windows still apply. Carefully plead the nature of the procedural defect and applicable timing/standing predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unresolved question — notice of correction vs notice of change
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a 'notice of correction' (a category used by the Department of State in the FAR) constitutes a 'notice of change' triggering the fourth point of entry is unsettled by the Florida Pulp & Paper decision and remains a source of uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Department of State considers notices of correction 'useful' and recommends agencies use them for technical corrections, their routine use can blur statutory text requiring publication of substantive changes. Parties should assess the content of any 'notice of correction' to determine whether it effectuated a substantive change (and thus triggered the fourth window) and be prepared to litigate that issue if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice — file at earliest available opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the court permitted reliance on later points of entry, one judge noted that 'a prudent person will file a rule challenge petition at the first available opportunity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing at the earliest applicable point minimizes risk of procedural dismissal or later limitations on grounds that can be challenged (for example, preserving ability to challenge provisions that are later characterized as unchanged).
